titleStmt.title: Environmental DNA (eDNA) detection and habitat occupancy of threatened spotted gar (Lepisosteus oculatus)

analytic.title: Environmental DNA (eDNA) detection and habitat occupancy of threatened spotted gar (Lepisosteus oculatus)

biblStruct.note: Received 15 March 2015; Revised 02 September 2015; Accepted 03 December 2015

div.p: 1. Determining the occurrence and site occupancy of rare and endangered species can be challenging, particularly without causing harm or stress to the species of concern.

2. Environmental DNA (eDNA) detection was used to assess habitat occupancy by spotted gar (Lepisosteus oculatus), which is federally listed as Threatened in Canada, with known occurrences limited to a small number of locations in southern Ontario.

3. Quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) assays were developed to detect spotted gar eDNA, which was detected in all but one previously recorded location. The eDNA method was shown to be more effective than traditional netting for detecting spotted gar habitat use.

4. The use of qPCR allowed for quantification of substantial variation in detection strength (copy number) among replicate eDNA samples, with implications for establishing sampling designs for detection and surveillance.

5. The use of eDNA for detection and monitoring of aquatic species of conservation concern shows great potential as a non-invasive method for assessing species occurrences and habitat occupancy, as well as for informing targeted sampling by conventional capture methods.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: Global biodiversity is experiencing accelerating losses from human impacts on environments and ecosystems (Butchart et al., 2010). While many conservation efforts have focused on terrestrial systems, higher trajectories of species loss in freshwater ecosystems indicate urgent conservation needs (Abell, 2002;Strayer and Dudgeon, 2010).

Freshwater fishes alone comprise one quarter of living vertebrate species, and recent assessments suggest that more than 30% are threatened (Singh, 2002). The rapid decline of North American freshwater fish diversity has continued despite increased knowledge and implementation of environmental and species protection laws (Jelks et al., 2008;Williams et al., 2011). Knowledge of a species' distribution and abundance is vital to understanding their ecology, and critical for conserving populations (Thompson, 2004).

Canada's Species at Risk Act (SARA) legislates the protection of critical habitat, which is habitat required for persistence of listed threatened or endangered species (S.C. 2002, c.29;Rosenfeld and Hatfield, 2006). As critical habitat can vary substantially among different life stages, defining and mapping it can be challenging (Rosenfeld and Hatfield, 2006). The information required to define critical habitat can be costly and time consuming to obtain, particularly in complex aquatic ecosystems (Ficetola et al., 2008;Takahara et al., 2012).

The use of environmental DNA (eDNA) is an emerging method for detecting the presence of low-abundance aquatic species that has applications for identifying occurrences of rare or endangered species, as well as invasive species during early colonization stages (Ficetola et al., 2008;Takahara et al., 2012;Thomsen et al., 2012;Biggs et al., 2015). Although eDNA has largely been used for invasive species surveillance (Ficetola et al., 2008;Jerde et al., 2011;Dejean et al., 2012), the method's sensitivity also makes it valuable for detecting rare species where they are present at low densities and difficult to find (Thompson, 2004;Thomsen et al., 2012;Janosik and Johnston, 2015;Laramie et al., 2015;Sigsgaard et al., 2015). Habitat sampling using eDNA has distinct advantages over traditional sampling methods such as netting that rely on invasive and/or selective capture, as DNA from sloughed tissues is collected from water samples without having to capture or directly encounter the species of interest (Darling and Mahon, 2011;Jerde et al., 2011;Sigsgaard et al., 2015). Thus, noninvasive species detections using eDNA have the additional benefit of avoiding any potential stress or mortality caused by sampling (Putman, 1995;Olson et al., 2012;Thomsen et al., 2012). As well as providing clear benefits for documenting occurrences of species of conservation concern, eDNA detections can also focus conservation efforts at appropriate sites and enable population monitoring with less cost and effort than relying solely on traditional sampling methods (Ficetola et al., 2008;Dejean et al., 2011, Sigsgaard et al., 2015).

The spotted gar (Lepisosteus oculatus) is a North American freshwater fish with a distribution that is largely limited to the Mississippi River basin and the Gulf of Mexico, but also includes disjunct populations in the Great Lakes basin (Figure 1; Page and Burr, 1991). The spotted gar is designated as Threatened within Canada, with only three confirmed populations: Long Point Bay, Pelee National Park, and Rondeau Bay in Lake Erie (COSEWIC, 2005). There are also recent records from the Bay of Quinte and Hamilton Harbour in Lake Ontario, and historic records from Lake St Clair (COSEWIC, 2005).

Major threats to the species in Canada include pollution and habitat loss, as adult spotted gar prefer shallow, clear, vegetated habitat within lakes and rivers (Glass et al., 2012;Gray et al., 2012). As the spotted gar is listed under Canada's federal Species at Risk Act (SARA), a recovery strategy must be developed and implemented for the species, including identification and protection of critical habitat (Department of Fisheries and Oceans, DFO, 2010). Current data on the species' distribution, abundance, and habitat use is vital for developing the recovery strategy.

In this study, quantitative eDNA methods were used to document the occurrence of DNA from spotted gar in historically identified habitats across its Canadian range and infer habitat use or occupancy to help inform conservation efforts for this threatened species. The objectives of this study were to: (1) test the effectiveness of the eDNA detection method for species-specific detection of spotted gar; (2) assess the presence of spotted gar in historical and contemporary sites in south-western Ontario; and (3) assess detection power and repeatability of eDNA for potential application to other aquatic species of conservation concern.

div.head: Field sampling
div.p: Locations with known and historically documented occurrences of spotted gar in Canada (Table 1, Figure 1) were sampled for eDNA testing. Long Point Bay, Hillman Marsh, Point Pelee, and Rondeau Bay in Lake Erie; the Thames River, a tributary to Lake St Clair; and, Hamilton Harbour in Lake Ontario (Figure 1) were all targeted for sampling based on historical and recent records (Table 1, COSEWIC, 2005;Bouvier and Mandrak, 2010;Department of Fisheries and Oceans, DFO, 2010;Staton et al., 2012).

To compare detection sensitivity of eDNA versus conventional sampling, nearshore habitats within Long Point Bay were also sampled using 1.2 m fine-mesh (6.35 mm bar mesh) fyke nets. A total of 47 fyke net sets, averaging 24 h, were set at multiple sites in Long Point Bay between 28 May and 7 June 2012, during the known spawning season for spotted gar (Tyler and Granger, 1984;Snedden et al., 1999;Glass et al., 2012). Netting sites were chosen based on identified critical habitat and areas considered to potentially support spotted gar (Department of Fisheries and Oceans, DFO, 2010;Staton et al., 2012). Nets were placed in shallow areas adjacent to shore to target spawning-related movements and left for 24 h (range 18.5-38 h owing to weather conditions). All nets and sampling gear were bleached and rinsed after retrieval to prevent DNA cross-contamination. The netting was conducted under a Species at Risk scientific permit issued by Fisheries and Oceans Canada (DFO), and was done in accordance with guidelines set by the DFO's Canada Centre for Inland Waters Animal Care Committee (Protocol Number: AUP # 1017). Water samples for eDNA testing were collected at each recent and historically known location for spotted gar (Table 1, Figure 1), sampling 10 sites within each general location and taking five replicate 1 L water samples per site. For the Thames River, three 1 L water samples were collected from each of 16 sites. Owing to logistical delays, water sampling was carried out from 19-25 June 2012 instead of coinciding with the netting effort. All sampling followed protocols established by Mahon et al. (2010), which include multiple safeguards and quality checks to reduce contamination and minimize the possibility of false positive results (Mahon et al., 2010). Post-collection samples were stored in 60 L coolers with ice packs to prevent DNA degradation. Negative controls (one 1 L sample of clean water per cooler) were also brought into the field to test for contamination from handling among environmental samples. As described above, all sampling gear was bleached and rinsed between locations to prevent DNA cross-contamination. Three 1 L water samples were collected from the Otonabee River (Peterborough, Ontario) to act as field controls, since there are no known or historical records of spotted gar within the Otonabee River. These precautions are necessary because of the high sensitivity of polymer chain reaction (PCR), which can make it prone to contamination during field sampling or laboratory processing (Darling and Mahon, 2011).

div.head: Filtering
div.p: Water samples were filtered within 3-18 h of collection. Water was filtered using a filter funnel attached to a vacuum source, with two types of fine-pore filters: 1.0 μm pore size Whatman TM 47 mm GF/B filters and 1.2 μm pore Whatman TM 47 mm GF/C filters. Previous work under controlled conditions showed that DNA yields from these two filter types were not significantly different (C. Wilson, unpubl. data). All filters were stored at -80°C until extracted to prevent DNA degradation (Anchordoquy and Molina, 2007).

div.head: Extractions
div.p: DNA was extracted from the water filters using MoBio Power Water extraction kits. The manufacturer's extraction protocol was followed with the following modifications: (1) extractions were made in 15 mL tubes rather than the bead tubes provided; (2) samples were agitated using an orbital shaker for 30 min rather than 5 min; (3) after the shaking stage for GF/C filters, an additional 500 μL of PW1 was added and the samples were vortexed; and (4) final elution was done with low TE (10 mmol L -1 Tris pH 8, 0.1 mmol L -1 EDTA) instead of the PW6 solution provided. Extracted samples were stored at -20°C to prevent DNA degradation. Genomic DNA was also extracted from 12 reference samples of spotted gar (fin clips preserved in 80% ethanol) from several Lake Erie locations (Point Pelee, Long Point, Rondeau Bay) and Missouri, USA using an alkali extraction protocol (Dissing et al., 1996).

Successful extraction of DNA for both reference and environmental samples was confirmed by gel electrophoresis, visualizing 2 μL of DNA from each extraction with SYBR Green stain in a 1.5% agarose gel alongside a 100 bp mass ladder (Bioshop Canada). qPCR Quantitative PCR (qPCR) was used to test the detection efficacy of spotted gar eDNA, using species-specific primers and probe designed to amplify and detect a 61 bp segment of the mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase I (COI) gene based on L. oculatus sequences in BOLD (Ratnasingham and Hebert, 2007). The COI gene is well-suited for eDNA detection of species of interest, based on species-diagnostic differences between most species and the rapidly growing global database of DNA barcodes based on COI sequences (Hebert et al., 2003;Ratnasingham and Hebert, 2007). The barcoding region of COI has the additional benefit of being flanked by two highly conserved 'universal' primer sites for PCR, which simplifies obtaining DNA barcodes from novel species of interest (Hebert et al., 2003).

The TaqMan-labelled qPCR probe was designed to have three mismatches from longnose gar (L. osseus), the only other gar species with a Canadian distribution (Page and Burr, 1991). All qPCR reactions were run with TaqMan® chemistry with a total reaction volume of 20 μL consisting of 5 μL undiluted DNA, 10 μL of TaqMan® Fast Advanced Master Mix (Applied Biosystems), 0.4 μL each for the qPCR primers and probe [S.GarTaqManF (5′-CTGACTTCTCCCACCCTCATTT-3′), 0.2 μL S.GarTaqManR (5′-CGGCCCCTGCTTCAAT C-3′), 0.2 μL SpottedGarProbe (6FAM-TTCTCCT TTTAGCCTCATC-MGBNFQ)], and 3.8 μL ddH 2 O. Reactions were carried out in a StepOnePlus thermocycler (Life Technologies), using an initial denaturation at 95°C for 2 min, followed by 40 cycles of 95°C denaturation for 1 s and 60°C annealing for 20 s. Two replicate qPCR reactions were run for each sample, and two series of qPCR standards (10-fold dilution series of spotted gar COI PCR product from 10 6 to 10 0 copies per reaction) and two negative controls were run on all sample plates. The resulting standard curves were used to quantify starting copy number estimates of template DNA in the environmental samples. qPCR was also used to test a subset of environmental samples for inhibition using an Internal Positive Control (IPC; Life Technologies). For this subset of IPC controls, 20 μL qPCR reactions were run with TaqMan® chemistry, consisting of 5 μL undiluted DNA, 10 μL of TaqMan® Fast Advanced Master Mix (Applied Biosystems), 0.4 μL each of S.GarTaqManF, S. GarTaqManR, and SpottedGarProbe, 1.2 μL ddH 2 O, 2.2 μL of 10× Exo IPC Mix, and 0.4 μL 50× Exo IPC DNA.

div.head: Establishing a detection threshold
div.p: Determination of whether or not a result is a 'positive' detection requires careful interpretation and appropriate quality checks and controls. Darling and Mahon (2011) suggested defining a priori criteria and thresholds to distinguish clearly between positive and negative detections, minimize observer bias, and work toward consistent scoring and interpretation. For qPCR, the assay's sensitivity depends on many factors including sampling and DNA extraction procedures, target rarity in samples, presence of inhibitors, and amplification conditions (Foy and Parkes, 2001). Method sensitivity is associated with the detectable lower limit of the method, or the limit of detection (LOD), which can be defined to give insight into the lowest detection limit for a qPCR assay (Burns and Valdivia, 2008). Generally, the LOD is conveyed as the amount of analyte the analytical method detects successfully at a minimum 95% of the time (Ros-García et al., 2012). In the present study the 1 DNA copy/5 μL had a high failure rate (45%), resulting in the 10 DNA copies/5 μL being set as the LOD and threshold for detection. Confident detections were defined as samples that consistently amplified at or above the 10-copy detection threshold. If the samples showed qPCR detection while the negative field and laboratory control samples did not, it was inferred that spotted gar DNA was present at the sampling site.

div.head: Sequencing
div.p: A subset of samples with positive detections, including at least one positive from each site with positive detections, were amplified using conventional PCR primers developed for a 260 bp segment of spotted gar COI (Bronnenhuber and Wilson, 2013), bidirectionally sequenced using BigDye 3.1 sequencing chemistry (Applied Biosystems), and visualized on an AB3730 capillary sequencer (Applied Biosystems) to ensure that the amplified DNA was from spotted gar. In cases where multiple positive detections occurred at a site, a representative subsample was sequenced. All sequences were proofread using Sequencher 5.1 (Gene Codes, Inc.) and identified using the BLAST tool on Genbank (www.ncbi. nlm.nih.gov) to look for homologous sequences. Sequences were also visualized using MEGA version 5 (Tamura et al., 2011) alongside samples from spotted gar and longnose gar obtained from Genbank and BOLD (Ratnasingham and Hebert, 2007) to confirm species identity of DNA from the environmental samples.

div.head: Mean copy number
div.p: The mean copy number of target DNA within the environmental samples was calculated by taking the arithmetic mean of the qPCR replicates from all filters for each site. Any sites that had negative control samples amplified above the detection threshold (10 copies/5 μL) were assumed to be a result of error or contamination ('false positive' data; Darling and Mahon, 2011) and were therefore excluded from the mean calculation data.

div.head: Netting data
div.p: The 47 net sets over 6 sampling days (28-30 May, 5-7 June) in Long Point Bay captured a total of 7737 fish from 31 species (means and standard errors of 164.6 + 22.5 and 9.9 + 0.5 respectively; data not shown), including three longnose gar. Despite the extensive netting effort, only three spotted gar were captured, all of which were caught at Long Point Bay Site 2 (Figure 2).

div.head: eDNA detections
div.p: Spotted gar DNA was successfully amplified from sites within five of the six sampling locations Long Point Bay, (E) Thames River, and (F) Hamilton Harbour with detections categorized by samples yielding starting DNA copy numbers greater than 100 copies/5 μL in at least one sample (green), starting copy numbers greater than 10 copies/5 μL and less than 100 copies/5 μL in at least one sample (yellow), and no detection or starting copy numbers less than 10 copies/5 μL in all samples (red). The square symbol in Long Point Bay indicates the location where live spotted gar were captured.

(Figure 2), with positive detections at 30-90% of sampled sites. Detections were not uniform: DNA concentrations shown in Figure 2 represent maximum rather than mean values of DNA copy number detected from filters or qPCR replicates at each site. Sampling locations with positive detections had 1-8 sites below the cutoff detection threshold (≥10 copies/5 μL), 3-8 sites with eDNA detections between 10 and 100 copies/5 μL, and < 5 sites with eDNA detections greater than 100 copies/5 μL (Figure 2). No positive detections for spotted gar DNA were obtained from the Hamilton Harbour locations based on the predefined minimum detection threshold (Figure 2). Data from field samples associated with detections in negative cooler and filtering controls (14% of the negative controls) were excluded from the results. The field controls from the Otonabee River (outside the species range) did not yield positive detections, and the subset of samples tested using the exogenous Internal Positive Control showed no evidence of PCR inhibition.

The qPCR surveillance yielded reproducible results at control DNA concentrations down to 10 copies/5 μL and environmental samples at concentrations below 100 copies/5 μL (Figure 2). Several locations yielded at least one sample with an estimated DNA concentration between 10 and 100 copies/5 μL (Figure 2), despite lower mean concentrations (Figure 3). Although qPCR results from a number of locations yielded putative detections of spotted gar DNA at concentrations below 10 target copies/5 μL (Figure 3), these were not considered to be positive detections as they fell below the predefined detection threshold.

All positive eDNA results that were sequenced matched reference spotted gar sequences obtained from GenBank, as well as the Canadian reference sequences in BOLD (Ratnasingham and Hebert, 2007). The amplified region had nine speciesdiagnostic mismatches between the reference sequences for spotted and longnose gar. The environmental sequences showed 96-100% homology with spotted gar, compared with a maximum homology of 95% with longnose gar.

div.head: Mean copy number
div.p: Replicate samples within sites exhibited substantial variation in DNA yield, despite water samples being taken in close proximity to each other (≤50 m) within a site (Figure 3). In general, sites with a higher mean number of copies of spotted gar eDNA had greater within-site variability (Figure 3). Both within and among sampling sites, a small fraction of the replicate samples consistently had high copy number detections (Figure 2) with the remaining replicates having low copy number detections (Figure 3).

div.head: DISCUSSION
div.p: This study demonstrated that eDNA is an effective tool for documenting occurrences and habitat occupancy of spotted gar, and showed eDNA detection success similar to other freshwater studies with locations known to be inhabited by the species having high detection success (Goldberg et al., 2011;Thomsen et al., 2012;Biggs et al., 2015;Janosik and Johnston, 2015). This study differed somewhat from most other eDNA studies on species at risk by its scale, documenting positive detections over most of the species' Canadian range.

Spotted gar DNA was successfully detected at all sampled Lake Erie locations (Hillman Marsh, Point Pelee, Long Point Bay, Rondeau Bay), as well as the Thames River. There have been recent collections of spotted gar at these locations, excluding the Thames River (Table 1; Department of Fisheries and Oceans, DFO, 2010;Glass et al., 2012). In addition, the rates and levels of eDNA detection were generally consistent with what is known about spotted gar abundance in the sampled locations, with the exception of sites in the Thames River and Hamilton Harbour (discussed below). Three locations (Hillman Marsh, Point Pelee, Rondeau Bay) had detections at a majority of the sites sampled. Rondeau Bay and Point Pelee also have the largest population estimates for spotted gar in Ontario, the population status of these populations were assessed as 'good' and 'fair', respectively (Table 1; Department of Fisheries and Oceans, DFO, 2010). Other studies similarly found that detection rates were higher in areas with higher density estimates for target organisms (Pilliod et al., 2013;Laramie et al., 2015). While collection data for spotted gar are limited at Hillman Marsh, the habitat is suitable for spotted gar (Snedden et al., 1999;Ostrand et al., 2004;Glass et al., 2012), and spotted gar have been captured in the area (Table 1, N. Mandrak, unpublished data 2012). Long Point Bay had DNA detections at three of 10 sampled sites; by contrast, netting efforts for spotted gar within the bay met with minimal success, resulting in the population status being categorized as 'poor' (Table 1, Department of Fisheries and Oceans, DFO, 2010). In 2010, 129 fyke net sets targeting the species caught only six individuals, and only 17 adults had been captured before then (Glass and Mandrak, 2014). The limited number of site detections in Long Point Bay may therefore reflect a low density of spotted gar in the area; other studies have demonstrated increased probability of detection with increasing density or biomass of the target species (Pilliod et al., 2013;Takahara et al., 2013;Moyer et al., 2014).

The detection of spotted gar DNA at eight of the 16 sites sampled within the Thames River was unexpected, as spotted gar are considered to be extirpated within the Lake St. Clair catchment (Table 1; COSEWIC, 2005; Department of Fisheries and Oceans, DFO, 2010). Although there is one historical record for spotted gar from the Thames River area of Lake St Clair, none have been recorded for over half a century (COSEWIC, 2005). Follow-up netting in 2013 (40 24 h fyke net sets, 365 m of trammel net, and 1530 s of boat electrofishing) in the vicinity of the positive eDNA detections failed to detect spotted gar, although 27 species including more than 400 longnose gar were captured (Marson et al., 2014). Similar species detections using eDNA have been reported from other studies sampling for rare and long-unobserved fish species: Janosik and Johnston (2015) reported detection of eDNA from the slackwater darter (Etheostoma boschungi) at a site with no record since 1970, and Sigsgaard et al. (2015) detected European weather loach (Misgurnis fossilis) eDNA at a site where the species had not been observed for 20 years. These support the use of eDNA as a highly sensitive detection method for aquatic organisms, allowing detection of rare species in areas that went many years without record.

Although recent sampling yielded many longnose gar and no spotted gar from the Thames River (Marson et al., 2014), the possibility that the qPCR tests could have amplified eDNA from longnose gar despite primer and probe mismatches was excluded by sequence confirmation of positive eDNA results as belonging to L. oculatus (98-100% homology to spotted gar reference sequences). As previous studies have demonstrated that hybridization among gars can occur, it is possible that the eDNA detections were from hybrid fish with spotted gar maternal ancestry (Herrington et al., 2008).

Despite records of spotted gar in Hamilton Harbour (COSEWIC, 2005), eDNA sampling failed to detect its presence. The lack of detection may have resulted from spotted gar leaving the area after spawning, as the harbour was the last location sampled and sampling occurred almost a month after the peak spawning time for spotted gar (Tyler and Granger, 1984). General observations of spotted gar have documented spawning along the shore (where current eDNA sampling occurred) in the spring, followed by post-spawning movement into the broader lake habitat (Snedden et al., 1999;Glass et al., 2012). This underscores the importance of a strong spatio-temporal sampling design (Darling and Mahon, 2011): repeated sampling throughout the year would also provide insight into seasonal variation in habitat occupancy, which would provide important information when establishing critical habitat for protected species. The apparent lack of detection of spotted gar DNA in Hamilton Harbour may also have been due to the detection threshold used (10 copies/5 μL), potentially excluding valid low-quantity detections. This is a recognized shortcoming of measures to prevent false positives, which can create a bias towards the error of false negative detections (Darling and Mahon, 2011). Despite this possibility, having an a priori cutoff threshold is a necessary precaution to safeguard against false positives from potential contamination, and enable robust confidence in positive detections (Darling and Mahon, 2011).

The successful detection of spotted gar DNA at five of the six sampled locations highlights that eDNA can be used as a tool to detect rare species in both lentic and lotic environments. To date, many eDNA studies have focused on small lentic pond environments (Ficetola et al., 2008;Dejean et al., 2012;Takahara et al., 2013). eDNA detectability in lotic environments is probably influenced by additional factors such as flow (Deiner and Altermatt, 2014;Laramie et al., 2015;Strickler et al., 2015). Although eDNA studies within lotic systems have reported successful detection of rare species (Goldberg et al., 2011;Thomsen et al., 2012;Jane et al., 2015;Laramie et al., 2015), studies focusing on lentic environments have often reported more consistent success rates (Ficetola et al., 2008;Thomsen et al., 2012). Detection of spotted gar where they are considered extirpated, and thus presumably present at low density, suggests that the eDNA method may be used as a highly sensitive method of rare species detection, even within lotic environments.

A criticism and perceived limitation of using eDNA as a monitoring tool for rare and invasive species is that eDNA detections identify the presence of the target species' DNA rather than individuals themselves (ECALS, Environmental DNA Calibration Study, 2013). Posited alternative sources of DNA include carcasses, effluent from live food markets and pet shops, sewer runoff, bird droppings, or contaminated sampling gear (Darling and Mahon, 2011;ECALS, Environmental DNA Calibration Study, 2013, Merkes et al., 2014). As the spotted gar is a rare and protected species in Canada, however, it is unlikely that the positive DNA detections in this study resulted from any of these sources. As it is illegal to trade native fish species in Canada, spotted gar is protected under SARA, and the gar pet trade largely consists of the similar-looking but genetically divergent Florida gar (Lepisosteus platyrhincus). Spotted gar is a rare top-level predator; although limited bird predation may occur on juvenile gar (Page and Burr, 1991), it is unlikely that DNA was transported via bird droppings, particularly over large distances or into novel locations. Thus, positive eDNA detections should be reliable indicators of the occurrence of spotted gar in or near sampled areas, and similar arguments would hold for other endangered taxa.

For eDNA to be accepted as a valid monitoring technique, it must meet a number of criteria including accuracy, precision, and repeatability (Invasive Species Advisory Committee, ISAC, 2012). The substantial variation observed among replicate samples within detection sites has been reported in other studies as well (Ficetola et al., 2008(Ficetola et al., , 2015;;Foote et al., 2012;Klymus et al., 2015). Variability among replicate samples could be contributed to by non-homogeneous mixing, heterogeneity of fish distribution in the water column, or inefficiencies in DNA extraction and testing (Goldberg et al., 2011;Mahon et al., 2013;Eichmiller et al., 2014). The number of positive detections among replicate samples provides an estimate of detection probability, which is valuable for designing efficient sampling protocols.

Detection probability is likely to vary based on species characteristics, local density, and sampling location; therefore, ideal replicate numbers will probably be study-specific (Darling and Mahon 2011;Takahara et al., 2012;Moyer et al., 2014). For example, Schmidt et al. (2013) found that the detection probability for Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis increased with the number of replicate water samples taken, with a plateau at five for robust detection. For community 'metabarcoding' (multispecies detection from eDNA samples via next-generation sequencing) Ficetola et al. (2015) suggested that the number of replicates should vary with detection probability, with a minimum of eight needed for species with low detection probabilities (<0.5) to limit false absences. As pointed out by Pilliod et al. (2013) and Jane et al. (2015), detection probability is also expected to vary with source biomass.

The variation in detection strengths within and among sites also indicates potential limitations in spatial resolution for mapping habitat use with eDNA. In systems where both target (source species) movements and sampling medium (water) are literally fluid, detection levels should not be overinterpreted. Because eDNA and fish both move, inferences from this study should probably be made at the larger location scale (local bay/harbour/river) rather than individual sites sampled within general locations. In standing water environments such as small ponds (Dejean et al., 2011;Takahara et al., 2012Takahara et al., , 2013;;Eichmiller et al., 2014;Moyer et al., 2014) and simple stream systems (Goldberg et al., 2011), site detections may sufficiently represent sampled habitats. Patchy distribution of eDNA detections has also been reported for common carp (Cyprinus carpio), with significantly higher eDNA detection rates in high-use areas (Eichmiller et al., 2014). In larger water bodies, however, eDNA detection probabilities are influenced by a number of factors, including the distance from the source, site conditions, and number of fish present in the area (Darling and Mahon, 2011;Takahara et al., 2012). Care should therefore be taken in interpreting the spatial scale and resolution of results from larger flowing systems or water bodies, as detections at sampling points may reflect distant or upstream rather than local contributions (Deiner and Altermatt, 2014), and will also be influenced by flow rate and proximity or distance from biological sources (Pilliod et al., 2013;Jane et al., 2015;Klymus et al., 2015). Accordingly, more research is needed to strengthen the application of eDNA for identifying critical habitats sensu Rosenfeld and Hatfield (2006) for species of conservation concern.

The detection of spotted gar at the majority of their previously documented locations across their Canadian range (COSEWIC, 2005) has demonstrated the efficacy and sensitivity of eDNA surveillance for aquatic endangered species. Although this study supports the use of eDNA as a tool for monitoring and detecting aquatic endangered species to focus conservation efforts, eDNA surveillance should be used to augment and focus conventional sampling methods rather than replace them. The high variability within replicate samples and potential rejection of low-copy data demonstrate the limitations of current eDNA methodology, and it is unlikely to replace capture methods to provide information on population size or demographic structure. As this new methodology matures, collaborations between the scientific community and management agencies should work towards establishing rigorous protocols and thresholds to maximize the information benefits from eDNA studies. With thoughtful sampling design and validation testing, eDNA applications have excellent potential for documenting species occurrences and facilitating habitat protection for threatened and endangered species.
